title: The French Defense
subtitle: Build a pawn chain — then attack its base.
goals: Understand the French pawn chain and the bad bishop
Attack a chain at its base, not its head
Win a pawn when the base is under-defended

steps.say: The French Defense: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5. Black challenges the centre immediately, but at a price — the pawn on e6 locks in the light-squared bishop on c8. That bishop is the 'French bishop', and finding a job for it is Black's lifelong problem in this opening. In return, Black gets a rock-solid structure and a clear plan.
White's most direct try is the Advance Variation — push past and take the space. This creates a pawn CHAIN, and pawn chains have a rule: you cannot attack the head, so you attack the base.

autoMoves.say: 3.e5 — White gains space and shuts the centre. The chain is d4-e5, and its base is d4.
3...c5! Immediately hitting the base of the chain. Not the e5 pawn — that one is defended and hard to reach — but d4, which holds everything up.
White props up d4 with another pawn...
...and Black adds a second attacker to d4.
A third attacker on d4, and the queen on b6 also eyes the b2 pawn. The entire opening battle is now about one square.

steps.say: Count the d4 square: White defends it with the c3 pawn and the f3 knight — two. Black attacks it with the c5 pawn, the c6 knight and the b6 queen — three. White must add a defender, and the natural developing move does not do that. Watch.
White develops the bishop — a perfectly natural move that ignores the argument on d4.

autoMoves.say: 6.Bd3? The bishop looks great on the b1-h7 diagonal, and it defends absolutely nothing on d4.

steps.prompt: White ignored the base of the chain. Win the d4 pawn — it takes three accurate moves.
hints: Don't start with the knight. Clear the c3 pawn out of the way first, so that d4 loses a defender.
cxd4 cxd4, and now d4 is defended only by the f3 knight but attacked by your knight AND your queen.
cxd4 cxd4 Nxd4! and the recapture Nxd4 runs into Qxd4 — you come out a clean pawn up.

line.say: First, trade off the propping pawn. White must recapture...

Now the counting works. White's f3 knight recaptures, but then your queen on b6 takes on d4 — and there is no third defender. A clean extra pawn, and White's e5 pawn is left weak with its base gone. Note the move order: taking with the knight FIRST would have failed, because the c3 pawn was still guarding d4.

rejections.say: Too early. The c3 pawn still defends d4, so after cxd4 you have simply given away a knight for a pawn. Exchange on d4 with the c-pawn FIRST to remove that defender.
The b2 pawn is a distraction, and after Nbd2 your queen can find itself short of squares. The real target is the base of the chain — start with the pawn exchange on d4.
Attacking the bishop instead of the pawn lets White play Be2 and consolidate the centre. The whole plan of the French is d4 — three attackers against two defenders, once the c-pawns come off.
Developing the bad bishop is a real French idea, but not while a pawn is hanging by a thread. Cash in on d4 now — the counting favours you only for this one move.

steps.wrongSay: d4 has two defenders (c3 and Nf3) and three attackers. Which capture removes a defender before you take with a piece?
steps.successSay: That's the French in one rule: never attack the head of a pawn chain, always the base — and trade off its supports before you take.
